notes.h: Systems, properties and the state of a pure substance
notes.body:
A thermodynamic system is the matter (closed system or control mass) or region of space (open system or control volume) chosen for analysis; everything outside it is the surroundings. Properties describe its state. Intensive properties such as temperature T, pressure p, density ρ and specific volume v do not depend on the size of the system; extensive properties such as mass, volume V and internal energy U do. Dividing an extensive property by mass gives a specific property (v = V/m, u = U/m).

- State postulate: the state of a simple compressible substance is fixed by two independent intensive properties.
- Zeroth law: two bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other. This is what makes thermometry possible. Always use kelvin in thermodynamic relations: T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
- Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure. Tables and gas laws need absolute values.

Phase change. On T–v and p–v diagrams the saturation dome separates compressed liquid, the wet (two-phase) region and superheated vapour. The dome peaks at the critical point (water: 22.06 MPa, 373.95 °C). Inside the dome T and p are tied together (T = T_sat(p)), so they are not independent and a second property is needed:
- Quality x = m_vapour/m_total, and any specific property y = y_f + x·y_fg, where y_fg = y_g − y_f.
- Compressed liquid is normally approximated as saturated liquid at the same temperature: v ≈ v_f(T), u ≈ u_f(T).

Ideal gas: pv = RT or pV = mRT, with R = R̄/M (R̄ = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K; for air R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K). For an ideal gas u and h depend only on T: du = c_v dT, dh = c_p dT, c_p − c_v = R and k = c_p/c_v (about 1.4 for air near room temperature). The compressibility factor Z = pv/RT measures real-gas behaviour. The ideal model works at low reduced pressure or high reduced temperature and fails near the saturation dome.

Worked example. A 0.6 m³ rigid vessel holds 2 kg of water at 200 kPa, so v = 0.3 m³/kg. This lies between v_f = 0.001061 and v_g = 0.8858 m³/kg, so the vessel holds a wet mixture at T_sat = 120.2 °C. Then x = (0.3 − 0.001061)/0.8847 = 0.338, so 0.68 kg is vapour, while the 1.32 kg of liquid fills only about 1.4 litres. With u_f = 504.5 and u_fg = 2024.6 kJ/kg, u = 1188.6 kJ/kg. Treating the steam as an ideal gas would predict about 605 kPa, roughly three times too high.

Common pitfalls:
- Putting gauge pressure or °C into pv = RT.
- Applying the ideal-gas law to steam close to saturation.
- Quoting a quality for compressed liquid or superheated vapour, where it is undefined.
- Interpolating across a phase boundary in the tables.

notes.h: The first law for closed and open systems
notes.body:
The first law is conservation of energy. With heat added to the system and work done by the system both taken as positive, a closed system obeys Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE. Joule's experiments in the 1840s showed that work and heat are interchangeable forms of energy transfer. Heat and work are path functions; U is a property.

Boundary work W_b = ∫p dV:
- constant pressure: W_b = p(V2 − V1)
- isothermal ideal gas: W_b = p1V1 ln(V2/V1)
- polytropic process pVⁿ = constant (n ≠ 1): W_b = (p2V2 − p1V1)/(1 − n)

Enthalpy h = u + pv groups internal energy with the flow work needed to push fluid across a boundary. For steady flow through a control volume the steady-flow energy equation (SFEE) is:

Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[(h2 − h1) + (V2² − V1²)/2 + g(z2 − z1)]

Typical device idealisations:
- Nozzles and diffusers: Q̇ ≈ Ẇ ≈ 0, so the enthalpy change becomes a kinetic energy change.
- Turbines, compressors and pumps: usually adiabatic, so Ẇ = ṁ(h1 − h2). For a liquid pump, w ≈ vΔp.
- Throttling valves: h2 = h1 (isenthalpic). An ideal gas therefore keeps the same temperature, but a liquid flashing to vapour cools sharply.
- Heat exchangers: no work, and the energy gained by one stream equals the energy lost by the other if the shell is insulated.

Unsteady (uniform-flow) processes. When an evacuated, insulated rigid tank fills from a supply line, the energy balance gives u_tank = h_line. For an ideal gas with constant specific heats this means T_tank = k·T_line: the flow work done by the line heats the gas.

Worked example. Steam enters a turbine at 12 kg/s, 3 MPa and 400 °C (h1 = 3231.7 kJ/kg) at 50 m/s. It leaves at 10 kPa with h2 = 2550 kJ/kg at 150 m/s, and 200 kW of heat is lost. Δke = (150² − 50²)/2 = 10 000 J/kg = 10 kJ/kg. So Ẇ = 12(3231.7 − 2550 − 10) − 200 = 7860 kW, about 7.86 MW. The kinetic energy term changes the answer by only 1.5%, which is why it is often neglected. Check that before you drop it.

Common pitfalls:
- Mixing J/kg (from V²/2) with kJ/kg. Divide by 1000.
- Sign errors with Q and W, especially for compressors and heat losses.
- Using c_v instead of c_p (that is, u instead of h) for a flowing stream.
- Assuming adiabatic means isothermal, or that a throttle is isentropic.

The first law allows any energy conversion that balances. The second law says which direction processes can go.

- Kelvin–Planck statement: no cyclic device can produce net work while exchanging heat with only one reservoir. No heat engine is 100% efficient.
- Clausius statement: no cyclic device can move heat from a colder body to a hotter one with no other effect. A refrigerator needs a work input.
- The two statements are equivalent, because violating one lets you violate the other.

Carnot principles (Sadi Carnot, 1824): no engine working between two reservoirs can beat a reversible one, and all reversible engines between the same reservoirs have the same efficiency. With absolute temperatures:
- η_Carnot = 1 − T_L/T_H
- COP_R,rev = T_L/(T_H − T_L) and COP_HP,rev = T_H/(T_H − T_L)

Entropy. The Clausius inequality ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 leads to the property entropy, dS = δQ_rev/T. The general balance for a closed system is S2 − S1 = ∫δQ/T_b + S_gen, with S_gen ≥ 0. S_gen = 0 only for reversible processes. Irreversibilities include friction, heat transfer across a finite ΔT, unrestrained expansion and mixing.
- Gibbs (Tds) relations: T ds = du + p dv = dh − v dp.
- Ideal gas: s2 − s1 = c_p ln(T2/T1) − R ln(p2/p1). Isentropic with constant k: T2/T1 = (p2/p1)^((k−1)/k).
- Incompressible solid or liquid: Δs = c ln(T2/T1).
- Isentropic efficiencies: turbine η_T = (h1 − h2a)/(h1 − h2s); compressor η_C = (h2s − h1)/(h2a − h1).

Exergy is the maximum useful work obtainable as a system comes into equilibrium with a dead state at T0, p0. The Gouy–Stodola theorem gives the exergy destroyed as T0·S_gen. Second-law (exergetic) efficiency compares actual useful output with the reversible limit.

Worked example. Two 5 kg copper blocks (c = 0.385 kJ/kg·K) at 400 K and 300 K are placed in contact inside an insulated enclosure. They reach 350 K. S_gen = mc[ln(350/400) + ln(350/300)] = 1.925 × (−0.1335 + 0.1542) = 0.0397 kJ/K. That is positive, so the process is possible and irreversible. If a reversible engine ran between the blocks instead, the final temperature would be √(400 × 300) = 346.4 K and the engine could deliver 1.925 × (700 − 692.8) = 13.8 kJ of work.

Common pitfalls:
- Using °C in Carnot expressions.
- Saying a system's entropy can never fall. It can, when heat leaves the system. Only S_gen (or the entropy of an isolated system) cannot decrease.
- Treating 'adiabatic' and 'isentropic' as the same. An adiabatic process is isentropic only if it is also reversible.

The ideal Rankine cycle is the model for steam power plants: 1→2 isentropic pump, 2→3 constant-pressure heating in the boiler, 3→4 isentropic turbine expansion, 4→1 constant-pressure condensation.
- Pump work w_p ≈ v1(p2 − p1). It is small but must be included in h2.
- η = (w_t − w_p)/q_in, with q_in = h3 − h2.
- To raise efficiency: raise the boiler pressure and superheat temperature (this raises the mean temperature of heat addition), lower the condenser pressure, reheat between turbine stages (this also raises the exit quality and reduces blade erosion), and use regenerative feedwater heating.

The air-standard Brayton cycle models gas turbines: isentropic compression, constant-pressure heat addition, isentropic expansion, constant-pressure heat rejection.
- Ideal η = 1 − 1/r_p^((k−1)/k), where r_p is the pressure ratio.
- The back work ratio w_c/w_t is high (often 40–60%), so compressor and turbine isentropic efficiencies have a strong effect on net output.
- Regeneration helps only when the turbine exhaust is hotter than the compressor exit. In a combined cycle, the gas turbine exhaust raises steam for a Rankine bottoming cycle.

Reciprocating engines (air-standard):
- Otto (spark ignition): η = 1 − 1/r^(k−1), where r is the compression ratio.
- Diesel (compression ignition): η = 1 − (1/r^(k−1))·(r_c^k − 1)/[k(r_c − 1)], where r_c is the cutoff ratio. At equal r, Otto is more efficient, but diesel engines run at higher r without knock.

Vapour-compression refrigeration: 1 saturated vapour leaves the evaporator, 1→2 compression, 2→3 condensation to saturated liquid, 3→4 throttling with h4 = h3.
- COP_R = (h1 − h4)/(h2 − h1). COP_HP = (h2 − h3)/(h2 − h1) = COP_R + 1.
- A COP above 1 does not break any law. It is a ratio of heat moved to work input.

Worked example (ideal Rankine). Boiler at 8 MPa and 500 °C (h3 = 3399.5 kJ/kg, s3 = 6.7266 kJ/kg·K); condenser at 10 kPa (h_f = 191.81, h_fg = 2392.1, s_f = 0.6492, s_fg = 7.4996).
- x4 = (6.7266 − 0.6492)/7.4996 = 0.810, so h4 = 191.81 + 0.810 × 2392.1 = 2130.3 kJ/kg.
- w_p = 0.00101 × (8000 − 10) = 8.07 kJ/kg, so h2 = 199.9 kJ/kg.
- w_t = 1269.2 kJ/kg and q_in = 3199.6 kJ/kg, so η = (1269.2 − 8.1)/3199.6 = 39.4%.
- A 100 MW net plant needs 100 000/1261.1 = 79.3 kg/s of steam.

Common pitfalls:
- Leaving out pump work, or taking h2 = h1.
- Comparing a real cycle with a Carnot cycle using the wrong reservoir temperatures.
- Using cold-air-standard k = 1.4 when the question gives variable specific heats or tables.

notes.h: Fluid statics: pressure, manometry and submerged surfaces
notes.body:
In a fluid at rest there is no shear stress, so pressure acts normal to every surface and is the same in all directions at a point (Pascal's law). A force balance on a fluid element gives the hydrostatic equation dp/dz = −ρg, with z measured upward. For a liquid of constant density, p = p0 + ρgh at depth h below a surface at pressure p0.

Manometry. Start at one end of the manometer and add ρgh for each drop in level, subtract ρgh for each rise, and finish at the other end. Points at the same height in the same continuous fluid are at the same pressure. For a U-tube with manometer fluid m between two points in a pipe carrying fluid f at the same height: p1 − p2 = (ρ_m − ρ_f)gΔh. A mercury barometer (Torricelli) reads atmospheric pressure as ρ_Hg g h, about 760 mm Hg.

Forces on plane submerged surfaces:
- Resultant F = p_c A, where p_c = ρg h_c is the gauge pressure at the centroid.
- It acts at the centre of pressure, y_cp = y_c + I_xc/(y_c A), measured along the plane from the free surface. I_xc is the second moment of area about the centroidal axis (b h³/12 for a rectangle). The centre of pressure is always below the centroid, and it moves towards the centroid as depth increases.
- Use gauge pressure when atmosphere acts on both sides.

Curved surfaces: the horizontal component equals the force on the surface's vertical projection, and the vertical component equals the weight of fluid (real or imaginary) directly above the surface.

Buoyancy and stability:
- Archimedes' principle: F_B = ρ_fluid g V_displaced, acting at the centre of buoyancy (the centroid of the displaced volume).
- A fully submerged body is stable if its centre of gravity G is below its centre of buoyancy B.
- A floating body is stable if the metacentric height GM = BM − BG is positive, where BM = I_waterplane/V_displaced.

Worked example. A vertical gate 2 m wide and 3 m high has its top edge 1.5 m below a water surface and is hinged along that edge. h_c = 3 m and A = 6 m², so F = 1000 × 9.81 × 3 × 6 = 176.6 kN. I_xc = 2 × 3³/12 = 4.5 m⁴, so y_cp = 3 + 4.5/(3 × 6) = 3.25 m. Taking moments about the hinge, the horizontal force needed at the bottom edge is P = 176.6 × (3.25 − 1.5)/3 = 103.0 kN.

Common pitfalls:
- Placing the resultant at the centroid instead of the centre of pressure.
- Using vertical depth where the slant distance y is needed for inclined surfaces (h_c = y_c sin θ).
- Sign slips when stepping through a manometer.
- Mixing absolute and gauge pressures.

notes.h: Continuity, Bernoulli and the momentum equation
notes.body:
Conservation of mass for steady flow through a control volume: Σṁ_in = Σṁ_out, with ṁ = ρAV̄. For incompressible flow the volumetric flow rate is constant: Q = A1V1 = A2V2. Halving the diameter therefore quadruples the velocity.

The Bernoulli equation, p/ρ + V²/2 + gz = constant (or as heads, p/ρg + V²/2g + z = H), holds along a streamline for steady, incompressible, inviscid flow with no shaft work or heat transfer. It is an energy statement: pressure head, velocity head and elevation head trade off against each other.

Applications:
- Torricelli: a jet from an orifice a depth h below a free surface has V = √(2gh) (ideal).
- Pitot-static tube: V = √(2Δp/ρ), where Δp is stagnation minus static pressure.
- Venturi or orifice meter: Q = C_d A2 √[2Δp/(ρ(1 − β⁴))], where β = d2/d1 and C_d is the discharge coefficient (about 0.98 for a good venturi, about 0.6 for a sharp-edged orifice).

For real pipe systems use the extended energy equation:
p1/ρg + V1²/2g + z1 + h_pump = p2/ρg + V2²/2g + z2 + h_turbine + h_L
The hydraulic grade line (HGL) plots p/ρg + z. The energy grade line (EGL) lies V²/2g above it and falls in the flow direction because of losses.

The linear momentum equation for a steady control volume: ΣF = Σ(ṁV)_out − Σ(ṁV)_in, applied in each direction as a vector equation. ΣF includes pressure forces on the control surface, body forces and the reaction from any solid boundary. Typical results:
- A jet striking a flat plate normally: F = ρQV.
- A jet turned through 180° by a vane: F = 2ρQV (stationary vane).
- Forces on bends, nozzles and reducers come from a combination of pressure and momentum terms.

Worked example. A horizontal venturi narrows from 200 mm to 100 mm (β = 0.5). A mercury–water manometer shows a 250 mm difference. Δp = (13 600 − 1000) × 9.81 × 0.25 = 30.9 kPa. Ideal throat velocity V2 = √[2 × 30 902/(1000 × (1 − 0.0625))] = 8.12 m/s, so Q_ideal = 0.00785 × 8.12 = 0.0638 m³/s. With C_d = 0.98, Q = 0.0625 m³/s.

Common pitfalls:
- Applying Bernoulli across a pump or turbine, or through a region with large losses (sudden expansions, long pipes).
- Forgetting the (1 − β⁴) term, or using the wrong area.
- Mixing gauge and absolute pressures in momentum balances. Gauge is simplest, because atmosphere acts all round.
- Confusing the force on the fluid with the force on the solid. They are equal and opposite.

Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to shear. For a Newtonian fluid, τ = μ du/dy (Newton's law of viscosity), where μ is the dynamic viscosity (Pa·s) and ν = μ/ρ is the kinematic viscosity (m²/s). Water at 20 °C has μ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s. Non-Newtonian fluids, such as shear-thinning polymer solutions and Bingham plastics like toothpaste, do not follow this linear law. At a solid wall the fluid has zero velocity relative to the wall (the no-slip condition).

The Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν compares inertial with viscous forces (Osborne Reynolds' dye experiments, 1883). In pipes, flow is normally laminar below Re ≈ 2300 and turbulent above about 4000, with a transitional range in between.

Laminar, fully developed pipe flow (Hagen–Poiseuille):
- Parabolic velocity profile, with V_max = 2V̄.
- Q = πD⁴Δp/(128μL), so Δp = 128μLQ/(πD⁴).
- Darcy friction factor f = 64/Re.

Head loss in any pipe (Darcy–Weisbach): h_f = f (L/D) V²/2g.
- Turbulent f depends on Re and the relative roughness ε/D. Read it from the Moody chart (1944), solve the Colebrook equation (1939), 1/√f = −2.0 log10[(ε/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re√f)], or use Haaland's explicit approximation (1983).
- Minor losses from fittings, valves and entries: h_m = K V²/2g.
- For non-circular ducts use the hydraulic diameter D_h = 4A/P_wetted.
- Pump power: P = ρgQH/η, where H is the head the pump must supply.

Boundary layers (Prandtl, 1904): viscous effects are confined to a thin layer near a surface, and the flow outside it can be treated as inviscid. This is why Bernoulli works outside the layer. Dimensional analysis (Buckingham Pi theorem) groups n variables in k fundamental dimensions into n − k dimensionless groups. Model testing relies on matching those groups.

Worked example. Water (ρ = 998 kg/m³, μ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s) flows at 0.02 m³/s through 500 m of 100 mm commercial steel pipe (ε = 0.045 mm). V = 0.02/(π × 0.1²/4) = 2.55 m/s and Re = 2.54 × 10⁵, so the flow is turbulent with ε/D = 0.00045. Colebrook gives f ≈ 0.018, so h_f = 0.018 × 5000 × 2.55²/(2 × 9.81) ≈ 30 m of water, about 294 kPa.

Common pitfalls:
- Mixing up the Darcy and Fanning friction factors (f_Darcy = 4 f_Fanning). Check which one the chart or formula uses.
- Using f = 64/Re for turbulent flow.
- Viscosity unit slips: 1 cP = 10⁻³ Pa·s.
- Forgetting the exit velocity head or the minor losses in a system energy balance.

notes.h: Heat transfer: conduction, convection, radiation and exchangers
notes.body:
There are three modes of heat transfer:
- Conduction (Fourier's law): q = −k dT/dx, where k is the thermal conductivity (W/m·K).
- Convection (Newton's law of cooling): q = h(T_s − T_∞). The heat transfer coefficient h depends on the flow, the fluid and the geometry; it is not a material property.
- Radiation (Stefan–Boltzmann): q = εσ(T_s⁴ − T_sur⁴), with σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴ and temperatures in kelvin.

Thermal resistance networks. For steady one-dimensional flow with no heat generation, Q̇ = ΔT_overall/ΣR.
- Plane wall: R = L/(kA). Convection: R = 1/(hA).
- Cylindrical shell: R = ln(r2/r1)/(2πkL).
- Resistances add in series. In parallel, their reciprocals add.
- Critical radius of insulation for a cylinder: r_cr = k_ins/h. Below r_cr, adding insulation increases heat loss, because the extra surface area outweighs the added conduction resistance.

Transient conduction. When the Biot number Bi = hL_c/k_solid < 0.1 (L_c = V/A), the solid's temperature is nearly uniform and lumped capacitance applies: (T − T_∞)/(T_i − T_∞) = exp(−t/τ), with τ = ρcV/(hA). Above Bi ≈ 0.1, use one-term series solutions or Heisler charts.

Convection correlations use the Nusselt number Nu = hL/k_fluid, Reynolds number and Prandtl number Pr = c_pμ/k.
- Turbulent pipe flow (Dittus–Boelter, Re > 10 000): Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Prⁿ, with n = 0.4 when the fluid is heated and 0.3 when it is cooled.
- Laminar fully developed pipe flow: Nu = 3.66 (constant wall temperature) or 4.36 (constant heat flux).

Heat exchangers:
- Q̇ = UA ΔT_lm, with ΔT_lm = (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2), using the terminal temperature differences. Counterflow gives the largest ΔT_lm for given terminal temperatures. Multipass designs use a correction factor F.
- ε-NTU method, for when outlet temperatures are unknown: C = ṁc_p, NTU = UA/C_min, ε = Q̇/Q̇_max, with Q̇_max = C_min(T_h,in − T_c,in).
- Overall coefficient for a thin wall: 1/U = 1/h_i + R_f + 1/h_o (+ wall term), where R_f is the fouling resistance.

Worked example. A furnace wall has 0.2 m of refractory (k = 1.2), 0.1 m of insulation (k = 0.08) and a 5 mm steel skin (k = 45). Gas is at 900 °C (h = 50 W/m²·K) and ambient air is at 25 °C (h = 10). Per m², ΣR = 0.020 + 0.167 + 1.250 + 0.0001 + 0.100 = 1.537 m²·K/W, so q = 875/1.537 = 569 W/m². The outer skin sits at 25 + 569 × 0.1 = 82 °C. About 80% of the temperature drop happens across the insulation.

Common pitfalls:
- Confusing Nu (uses k of the fluid) with Bi (uses k of the solid).
- Using °C in radiation calculations.
- Pairing the wrong ends when computing ΔT_lm.
- Using lumped analysis when Bi > 0.1.

cards.b: An intensive property (T, p, ρ, v) does not depend on the size of the system. An extensive property (m, V, U, H) does. Dividing an extensive property by mass gives a specific property, which is intensive.
Two independent intensive properties fix the state. Inside the saturation dome, T and p are linked, so one of them has to be paired with something else, such as v or quality x.
If bodies A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This is the basis of temperature measurement.

cards.f: Quality x of a wet mixture
cards.b: x = m_vapour/m_total, between 0 (saturated liquid) and 1 (saturated vapour). Any specific property y = y_f + x·y_fg.
p_abs = p_gauge + p_atm. Gas laws and property tables need absolute pressure. A vacuum gauge reads p_atm − p_abs.

cards.f: Ideal-gas equation and the specific gas constant
cards.b: pv = RT (or pV = mRT), with R = R̄/M and R̄ = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K. For air, R ≈ 0.287 kJ/kg·K.
Z = pv/(RT). Z = 1 for an ideal gas. Large departures from 1 show real-gas behaviour, which matters most near the critical point and the saturation dome.

cards.f: How to approximate compressed liquid properties without compressed liquid tables
cards.b: Treat the liquid as saturated liquid at the same temperature: v ≈ v_f(T), u ≈ u_f(T). Enthalpy can be refined with h ≈ h_f(T) + v_f(p − p_sat).
About 22.06 MPa and 373.95 °C. Above it, liquid and vapour phases cannot be told apart and there is no latent heat.

cards.f: Relations between c_p, c_v, R and k for an ideal gas
cards.b: c_p − c_v = R and k = c_p/c_v. Both u and h depend only on T: du = c_v dT and dh = c_p dT.

cards.f: Why is the ideal-gas model poor for steam at 200 kPa, 120 °C?
cards.b: That state is on or near the saturation dome, where intermolecular forces matter. For a 0.3 m³/kg wet mixture, pv = RT overestimates the pressure about threefold.

cards.f: First law for a closed system
cards.b: Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE, with Q positive into the system and W positive when done by the system.
W_b = (p2V2 − p1V1)/(1 − n). When n = 1 (isothermal ideal gas), W_b = p1V1 ln(V2/V1).

cards.f: Definition of enthalpy and its physical meaning
cards.b: h = u + pv. It combines internal energy with the flow work needed to push a fluid element across a boundary, which makes it the natural property for open systems.
Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[Δh + ΔV²/2 + gΔz]. Watch the units: V²/2 comes out in J/kg.
h2 = h1 (isenthalpic). For an ideal gas the temperature stays the same. For real fluids it changes according to the Joule–Thomson coefficient.

cards.f: Specific work of an ideal liquid pump
cards.b: w ≈ v(p2 − p1). For water at 1 MPa rise, w ≈ 0.001 × 1000 = 1 kJ/kg.

cards.f: Filling an evacuated insulated rigid tank from a line
cards.b: Energy balance gives u_tank = h_line. For an ideal gas with constant c_p and c_v, T_tank = k T_line. Air from a 300 K line ends at about 420 K.
No. Both are path functions (inexact differentials, δQ and δW). Internal energy, enthalpy and entropy are properties, with exact differentials.
With no heat transfer or work: V2 = √(V1² + 2(h1 − h2)). A 100 kJ/kg enthalpy drop from rest gives about 447 m/s.
ṁ_h(h_h,in − h_h,out) = ṁ_c(h_c,out − h_c,in). The heat leaving the hot stream all goes to the cold stream.
No cyclic device can produce net work while exchanging heat with only one thermal reservoir. A heat engine must reject some heat.
Heat cannot pass from a colder body to a hotter one with no other effect. A refrigerator or heat pump needs a work input.
η = 1 − T_L/T_H, with temperatures in kelvin. It is the maximum possible efficiency for any engine working between two reservoirs.

cards.f: Reversible refrigerator and heat pump COPs
cards.b: COP_R = T_L/(T_H − T_L) and COP_HP = T_H/(T_H − T_L), so COP_HP = COP_R + 1.

cards.f: Entropy balance for a closed system
cards.b: ΔS = ∫δQ/T_b + S_gen, with S_gen ≥ 0. S_gen = 0 only for a reversible process.

cards.f: Entropy change of an ideal gas
cards.b: Δs = c_p ln(T2/T1) − R ln(p2/p1) = c_v ln(T2/T1) + R ln(v2/v1). Use absolute T and p.

cards.f: Isentropic relation for an ideal gas with constant k
cards.b: T2/T1 = (p2/p1)^((k−1)/k) = (v1/v2)^(k−1), and pv^k = constant.

cards.f: Isentropic efficiency of a turbine vs a compressor
cards.b: Turbine: η_T = (h1 − h2a)/(h1 − h2s), actual over ideal work. Compressor: η_C = (h2s − h1)/(h2a − h1), ideal over actual work.
Exergy destroyed equals T0·S_gen, where T0 is the dead-state (environment) temperature. It links entropy generation to lost work potential.

cards.f: An inventor claims 65% efficiency between 800 K and 300 K. Verdict?
cards.b: Impossible. The Carnot limit is 1 − 300/800 = 62.5%, and no engine can exceed it.
Yes, if it rejects heat. What cannot be negative is entropy generation, so the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

cards.f: Four processes of the ideal Rankine cycle
cards.b: 1→2 isentropic pumping, 2→3 constant-pressure heat addition in the boiler, 3→4 isentropic expansion in the turbine, 4→1 constant-pressure condensation.

cards.f: Effect of reheat in a Rankine cycle
cards.b: It raises turbine exit quality (less blade erosion) and usually raises efficiency slightly, by increasing the mean temperature of heat addition.
η = 1 − 1/r_p^((k−1)/k). It depends only on the pressure ratio when specific heats are constant.
w_compressor/w_turbine. It is small in Rankine plants (around 1%) but large in gas turbines (often 40–60%), so component efficiencies matter far more in gas turbines.
η = 1 − 1/r^(k−1), where r is the compression ratio. With r = 10 and k = 1.4, η = 60.2%.

cards.f: Why do diesel engines often beat petrol engines in practice despite the lower Diesel-cycle η at equal r?
cards.b: They run at much higher compression ratios (about 15–22), because only air is compressed, so knock is not a limit.

cards.f: COP of a vapour-compression refrigerator from enthalpies
cards.b: COP_R = (h1 − h4)/(h2 − h1), with h4 = h3 after the throttle. State 1 is the evaporator exit and state 2 the compressor exit.

cards.f: Why use a throttle valve rather than an expansion turbine in refrigeration?
cards.b: The work an expander would recover from the wet, low-volume flow is small, and a valve is cheap, simple and controllable. The cost is some lost refrigeration effect.

cards.f: When is regeneration in a gas turbine beneficial?
cards.b: When the turbine exhaust is hotter than the compressor discharge. This is typical at low pressure ratios. At high r_p, the exhaust can be cooler and regeneration would heat the exhaust instead.
Hot gas turbine exhaust (often 500–600 °C) raises steam in a heat recovery steam generator, which drives a Rankine bottoming cycle and raises overall efficiency.
dp/dz = −ρg, with z upward. For a constant-density liquid, p = p0 + ρgh at depth h.
In a fluid at rest, the pressure at a point is the same in all directions, and a pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted throughout it.
p1 − p2 = (ρ_m − ρ_f)gΔh for two points at the same height in a fluid of density ρ_f, with manometer fluid ρ_m.

cards.f: Resultant force on a plane submerged surface
cards.b: F = ρg h_c A, where h_c is the depth of the centroid. It acts at the centre of pressure, which lies below the centroid.
y_cp = y_c + I_xc/(y_c A), measured along the plane from the free surface. I_xc = bh³/12 for a rectangle.
The buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced, F_B = ρ_f g V_disp, and acts through the centroid of the displaced volume.
Stable if the metacentric height GM = BM − BG > 0, with BM = I_waterplane/V_displaced.

cards.f: Vertical force on a curved submerged surface
cards.b: It equals the weight of fluid (real or imaginary) vertically above the surface, up to the free surface.

cards.f: Gauge pressure 10 m deep in seawater (ρ = 1025 kg/m³)
cards.b: p = 1025 × 9.81 × 10 = 100.6 kPa gauge, about one extra atmosphere. Absolute pressure is about 202 kPa.
Q = A1V1 = A2V2. Velocity is inversely proportional to area, so halving the diameter makes the flow 4 times faster.
Steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline, with no shaft work or heat transfer.
p/ρg + V²/2g + z = H (constant): pressure head plus velocity head plus elevation head.
V = √(2(p0 − p)/ρ), where p0 is the stagnation pressure and p the static pressure. A 5 kPa difference in water gives 3.16 m/s.
Q = C_d A2 √[2Δp/(ρ(1 − β⁴))], where β = d2/d1. C_d ≈ 0.98 for a venturi and about 0.6 for a sharp-edged orifice.
An ideal jet from an orifice a depth h below a free surface leaves at V = √(2gh), the same speed as free fall from height h.
ΣF = Σ(ṁV)_out − Σ(ṁV)_in, applied as vectors. ΣF includes pressure, body and wall forces acting on the control volume.

cards.f: Force of a jet striking a flat plate normally
cards.b: F = ρQV = ṁV, because all of the jet's momentum normal to the plate is destroyed.

cards.f: Hydraulic grade line vs energy grade line
cards.b: HGL = p/ρg + z. EGL = HGL + V²/2g. The EGL falls in the flow direction because of losses and jumps up at a pump.

cards.f: Why can't Bernoulli be applied across a sudden expansion?
cards.b: Turbulent mixing dissipates mechanical energy there. The loss (V1 − V2)²/2g has to be added, and it comes from combining the momentum and energy equations.
τ = μ du/dy. Dynamic viscosity μ is in Pa·s, and kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ is in m²/s.
Re = ρVD/μ. Pipe flow is laminar below about 2300 and turbulent above about 4000.
Δp = 128μLQ/(πD⁴) for laminar fully developed flow. Δp ∝ 1/D⁴, so halving D raises Δp 16-fold at the same Q.
h_f = f(L/D)(V²/2g). Laminar flow: f = 64/Re. Turbulent flow: f comes from the Moody chart or the Colebrook equation.
f_Darcy = 4 f_Fanning. Laminar flow: 64/Re (Darcy) or 16/Re (Fanning).
h_m = K V²/2g. K depends on the fitting. A sharp-edged entrance is about 0.5 and a pipe exit to a tank is 1.0.
D_h = 4A/P_wetted. Use it for non-circular ducts. For a circular pipe running full it equals D.
n variables involving k independent fundamental dimensions can be rearranged into n − k independent dimensionless groups.

cards.f: Velocity profile in laminar pipe flow
cards.b: Parabolic: u(r) = u_max(1 − r²/R²), with u_max = 2V̄. Turbulent profiles are much flatter.

cards.f: What does the Colebrook equation give, and why is it awkward?
cards.b: The turbulent Darcy f as a function of Re and ε/D. It is implicit in f, so it has to be solved by iteration or replaced by an explicit fit such as Haaland's.
At a solid surface the fluid velocity equals the wall's velocity. This sets up the velocity gradients that cause viscous shear and boundary layers.
q = −k dT/dx (W/m²). Heat flows down the temperature gradient. k is the thermal conductivity in W/m·K.

cards.f: Thermal resistance of a plane wall, a cylinder and a convective surface
cards.b: Wall: L/(kA). Cylinder: ln(r2/r1)/(2πkL). Convection: 1/(hA).

cards.f: Stefan–Boltzmann law for a grey surface in large surroundings
cards.b: q = εσ(T_s⁴ − T_sur⁴), with σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴. Temperatures must be in kelvin.

cards.f: Biot number and the lumped capacitance criterion
cards.b: Bi = hL_c/k_solid, with L_c = V/A. Lumped capacitance is valid when Bi < 0.1.
Nu = hL/k_fluid. It is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer across the fluid layer.
Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Prⁿ for turbulent pipe flow (Re > 10 000), with n = 0.4 when the fluid is heated and 0.3 when it is cooled.
ΔT_lm = (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2), where ΔT1 and ΔT2 are the temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger.
r_cr = k_ins/h. Insulating a pipe smaller than r_cr increases heat loss until the outer radius passes r_cr.
ε = Q̇/Q̇_max, with Q̇_max = C_min(T_h,in − T_c,in). Use it with NTU = UA/C_min when outlet temperatures are unknown.
Pr = c_pμ/k = ν/α, the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. It is about 0.7 for air and about 7 for water at room temperature.

questions.q: Which of the following is an intensive property?
questions.why: Specific volume (V/m) does not depend on how much substance there is. Volume, internal energy and mass all scale with the size of the system.

questions.q: An ideal gas is throttled adiabatically through a valve with negligible change in kinetic energy. Its temperature:
questions.why: Throttling is isenthalpic, h2 = h1. For an ideal gas h depends only on T, so T2 = T1.

questions.q: A heat engine runs between reservoirs at 800 K and 300 K. What is its maximum possible thermal efficiency?
questions.why: η_Carnot = 1 − T_L/T_H = 1 − 300/800 = 0.625. The 37.5% option is T_L/T_H, a common slip.

questions.q: An air-standard Otto cycle has a compression ratio of 10 and k = 1.4. Its thermal efficiency is closest to:
What is the gauge pressure 5 m below the free surface of water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
questions.why: p = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 5 = 49 050 Pa ≈ 49.1 kPa gauge. Adding atmospheric pressure would give about 150 kPa absolute.

questions.q: Water flows steadily through a pipe that narrows from 100 mm to 50 mm diameter. The mean velocity in the narrow section is:
questions.why: Q = AV is constant, and area scales with D², so halving D increases V by a factor of 4.

questions.q: In fully developed laminar flow at constant volumetric flow rate, the pipe diameter is halved. The pressure drop over the same length:
questions.why: Hagen–Poiseuille gives Δp = 128μLQ/(πD⁴), so Δp ∝ D⁻⁴ and (1/2)⁻⁴ = 16.

questions.q: Laminar pipe flow has Re = 1000. Using the Darcy–Weisbach equation, which friction factor should be used?
questions.why: For laminar flow f_Darcy = 64/Re = 0.064. The value 0.016 is the Fanning factor (16/Re), which would underestimate head loss fourfold in the Darcy–Weisbach equation.

questions.q: Lumped capacitance analysis of transient conduction is generally acceptable when:
questions.why: A Biot number below about 0.1 means internal conduction resistance is small compared with surface convection resistance, so the solid is nearly isothermal.

questions.q: A reversible heat pump keeps a house at 21 °C when the outside air is at 0 °C. Its coefficient of performance is closest to:
questions.why: COP_HP = T_H/(T_H − T_L) = 294.15/21 = 14.0. Using Celsius (21/21 = 1) gives the classic wrong answer.

questions.q: A rigid 0.4 m³ vessel contains 1.5 kg of water at 200 kPa. Given v_f = 0.001061 m³/kg and v_g = 0.8858 m³/kg at 200 kPa, determine the phase, the quality and the mass of vapour.
markScheme: v_f < v < v_g, so it is a saturated liquid–vapour mixture at T_sat ≈ 120.2 °C
questions.modelAnswer: The specific volume is v = V/m = 0.4/1.5 = 0.267 m³/kg. Because v_f < v < v_g, the vessel holds a wet mixture at the saturation temperature for 200 kPa (about 120.2 °C). The quality is x = (v − v_f)/(v_g − v_f) = (0.2667 − 0.00106)/0.8847 = 0.300, so the vapour mass is 0.300 × 1.5 = 0.450 kg and the remaining 1.05 kg is liquid. The liquid takes up only about 1.1 litres. Almost all of the volume is vapour even though most of the mass is liquid.

questions.q: Air in a piston–cylinder device is compressed polytropically (n = 1.3) from 100 kPa and 0.1 m³ to 0.02 m³. Find the final pressure and the boundary work, stating its sign.
markScheme: W_b ≈ −20.7 kJ: negative, so work is done on the gas
questions.modelAnswer: For a polytropic process p1V1ⁿ = p2V2ⁿ, so p2 = 100 × (0.1/0.02)^1.3 = 100 × 5^1.3 = 810 kPa. The boundary work is W_b = (p2V2 − p1V1)/(1 − n) = (810.3 × 0.02 − 100 × 0.1)/(1 − 1.3) = (16.21 − 10.00)/(−0.3) = −20.7 kJ. The negative sign, with the convention that work done by the system is positive, shows that about 20.7 kJ of work is done on the air during compression.

questions.q: An insulated, initially evacuated rigid tank is filled with air from a supply line at 300 K until the tank pressure equals the line pressure. Treating air as an ideal gas with k = 1.4, find the final air temperature in the tank and explain why it exceeds the line temperature.
markScheme: Uniform-flow energy balance with Q = W = 0 and m1 = 0 gives m2u2 = m_i h_i, so u2 = h_line
c_v T2 = c_p T_line, so T2 = k T_line = 1.4 × 300 = 420 K
The excess comes from flow work: the line gas pushes gas into the tank, and that pv work becomes internal energy
questions.modelAnswer: The control volume is the tank. There is no heat transfer, no shaft work and no initial mass, so the energy balance reduces to m2u2 = m_i h_i, giving u2 = h_line. For an ideal gas with constant specific heats, c_v T2 = c_p T_line, so T2 = k T_line = 1.4 × 300 = 420 K, or 147 °C. The gas ends up hotter than the line because each parcel entering carries its enthalpy, which includes flow work pv done by the gas behind it pushing it in. Once that parcel is inside the rigid tank, the flow work is stored as internal energy.

questions.q: Two 5 kg copper blocks (c = 0.385 kJ/kg·K), one at 400 K and one at 300 K, are brought into contact inside an insulated enclosure and reach equilibrium. Calculate the final temperature and the entropy generated, and comment on the result.
markScheme: Energy balance with equal masses: T_f = (400 + 300)/2 = 350 K
S_gen = +0.0397 kJ/K > 0, so the process is irreversible and allowed by the second law
questions.modelAnswer: The blocks have equal mass and specific heat, so the energy balance gives T_f = 350 K. Each block's entropy changes by mc ln(T2/T1), with mc = 1.925 kJ/K. The hot block changes by 1.925 ln(0.875) = −0.257 kJ/K and the cold block by 1.925 ln(1.1667) = +0.297 kJ/K. The enclosure is insulated, so all of the net change is generated: S_gen = 0.0397 kJ/K. This is positive, as the second law requires for heat transfer across a finite temperature difference. The hot block's entropy falls, which shows that an individual system's entropy can decrease.

questions.q: Explain how lowering the condenser pressure affects the thermal efficiency of a Rankine cycle, and give one practical drawback.
markScheme: Lower condenser pressure means a lower saturation temperature, so heat is rejected at a lower temperature
Turbine work rises, while heat input rises only slightly, so efficiency increases
Drawback: turbine exhaust quality falls, so more moisture erodes the last-stage blades
Other limits: the cooling-water temperature sets a minimum, and air leaks into the low-pressure condenser
questions.modelAnswer: Lowering the condenser pressure lowers the temperature at which heat is rejected. The expansion line extends further, so turbine work rises, while the heat input rises only a little (the pump exit enthalpy falls slightly). Net work rises faster than heat input, so efficiency improves, consistent with the Carnot idea of widening the temperature range. The drawback is that the turbine exhaust becomes wetter. Liquid droplets erode the low-pressure blades, and most designs aim to keep exit quality above about 0.88–0.90. The available cooling water temperature also sets a practical lower limit on condenser pressure.

questions.q: A U-tube manometer containing mercury (ρ = 13 600 kg/m³) is connected between two points at the same height in a horizontal water pipe. The mercury levels differ by 150 mm. Calculate the pressure difference between the points.
markScheme: Recognise that p1 − p2 = (ρ_m − ρ_w)gΔh for points at the same elevation
questions.modelAnswer: Step through the manometer from point 1 to point 2. The water columns above the mercury cancel except over the height Δh, where water sits in one leg and mercury in the other. So p1 − p2 = (ρ_m − ρ_w)gΔh = (13 600 − 1000) × 9.81 × 0.150 = 18 541 Pa ≈ 18.5 kPa. A common error is to use ρ_m alone, which gives 20.0 kPa and ignores the water in the manometer legs.

questions.q: A horizontal water jet (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) with a flow rate of 0.01 m³/s and a velocity of 20 m/s strikes a stationary flat plate held perpendicular to it, and the water leaves parallel to the plate. Find the force needed to hold the plate.
markScheme: Momentum equation in the jet direction: the incoming momentum flux is destroyed
F = 200 N, applied against the jet direction to hold the plate
questions.modelAnswer: Take a control volume around the plate. The water arrives with momentum flux ṁV in the jet direction and leaves along the plate with no component in that direction. Pressure is atmospheric everywhere on the control surface, so it contributes no net force. The momentum equation gives the force of the plate on the water as −ρQV, so the water pushes on the plate with ρQV = 1000 × 0.01 × 20 = 200 N. The support must supply 200 N acting against the jet.

questions.q: Define the Reynolds number for pipe flow, explain what it represents physically, and state the usual regime boundaries.
markScheme: It is the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces
Laminar below about 2300, turbulent above about 4000, transitional in between (sensitive to disturbances)
questions.modelAnswer: The Reynolds number is Re = ρVD/μ, where V is the mean velocity, D the pipe diameter and μ the dynamic viscosity. It measures the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in the flow. At low Re, viscosity damps disturbances and the flow stays laminar. At high Re, inertia amplifies them into turbulent eddies. For circular pipes, flow is normally laminar below about 2300 and turbulent above about 4000. In the range between, behaviour depends on the inlet conditions and disturbances.

questions.q: The pressure drop Δp in fully developed pipe flow depends on velocity V, diameter D, length L, density ρ, viscosity μ and wall roughness ε. Use the Buckingham Pi theorem to find a suitable set of dimensionless groups.
markScheme: 7 variables (Δp, V, D, L, ρ, μ, ε) and 3 dimensions (M, L, T), so 4 Pi groups
Choose repeating variables ρ, V, D
Groups: Δp/(ρV²), ρVD/μ = Re, L/D, ε/D
Result: Δp/(ρV²) = φ(Re, L/D, ε/D), consistent with Darcy–Weisbach (Δp ∝ f(Re, ε/D)·L/D·ρV²/2)
questions.modelAnswer: There are seven variables in three fundamental dimensions (M, L, T), so the theorem gives 7 − 3 = 4 independent groups. Taking ρ, V and D as repeating variables, the groups are: Π1 = Δp/(ρV²), a pressure coefficient; Π2 = ρVD/μ, the Reynolds number; Π3 = L/D; and Π4 = ε/D, the relative roughness. So Δp/(ρV²) = φ(Re, L/D, ε/D). Experiments show Δp is proportional to L/D for fully developed flow, which leads to the Darcy–Weisbach form Δp = f(Re, ε/D)(L/D)(ρV²/2).

questions.q: A steel ball bearing (D = 20 mm, ρ = 7800 kg/m³, c = 470 J/kg·K, k = 45 W/m·K) at 300 °C is cooled in air at 25 °C with h = 50 W/m²·K. Check that lumped analysis applies and find the time to reach 100 °C.
markScheme: Bi = hL_c/k = 50 × 0.00333/45 = 0.0037 < 0.1, so lumped analysis is valid
questions.modelAnswer: For a sphere, L_c = V/A = D/6 = 3.33 mm. Bi = 50 × 0.00333/45 = 0.0037, far below 0.1, so the ball is effectively isothermal. The time constant is τ = ρcV/(hA) = 7800 × 470 × 0.00333/50 = 244 s. From (T − T∞)/(T_i − T∞) = exp(−t/τ), t = 244 × ln(275/75) = 244 × 1.299 = 318 s, about 5.3 minutes. At 300 °C, radiation would add noticeably to the cooling, so this estimate is conservative (too long).

questions.q: Steam enters a turbine at 12 kg/s, 3 MPa and 400 °C (h1 = 3231.7 kJ/kg) with a velocity of 50 m/s. It leaves at 10 kPa with h2 = 2550 kJ/kg and a velocity of 150 m/s. The casing loses 200 kW to the surroundings. (a) Find the power output. (b) Find the exit quality and the exit flow area, given h_f = 191.81 kJ/kg, h_fg = 2392.1 kJ/kg, v_f = 0.00101 m³/kg and v_g = 14.670 m³/kg at 10 kPa. (c) Comment on whether neglecting kinetic energy would have been reasonable.
markScheme: States the SFEE with heat loss: Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[Δh + ΔV²/2]
Converts kinetic energy correctly: (150² − 50²)/2 = 10 000 J/kg = 10 kJ/kg
Correct sign on heat loss (Q̇ = −200 kW)
KE term is about 1.5% of the enthalpy drop, so neglecting it is reasonable for an estimate, but not when exit velocities are high
Large exit area shows why low-pressure stages are physically huge
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For a steady-flow control volume around the turbine, Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[(h2 − h1) + (V2² − V1²)/2], neglecting the change in potential energy. The kinetic energy term is (150² − 50²)/2 = 10 000 J/kg = 10 kJ/kg. Heat is lost, so Q̇ = −200 kW. Rearranging:

Ẇ = Q̇ − ṁ[(h2 − h1) + Δke] = −200 − 12[(2550 − 3231.7) + 10] = −200 + 12 × 671.7 = 7860 kW.

The turbine delivers about 7.86 MW.

(b) At 10 kPa, h2 = 2550 kJ/kg lies between h_f and h_g, so the exhaust is wet. x2 = (2550 − 191.81)/2392.1 = 0.986. Then v2 = 0.00101 + 0.986 × (14.670 − 0.00101) = 14.46 m³/kg. Continuity gives A2 = ṁv2/V2 = 12 × 14.46/150 = 1.16 m². This is a very large flow area, and it is why the last stages of condensing turbines have long blades and often split into parallel exhaust flows.

(c) Leaving out the kinetic energy change would give Ẇ = 12 × 681.7 − 200 = 7980 kW, an error of 120 kW, about 1.5%. That is acceptable for a first estimate. But exit velocities in low-pressure stages can reach 200–300 m/s, where the term becomes several per cent. The kinetic energy leaving the last stage is also a real 'leaving loss'. You should therefore check the magnitude before neglecting the term rather than assume it is negligible.

questions.q: The turbine from a steam plant expands steam from 3 MPa and 400 °C (h1 = 3231.7 kJ/kg, s1 = 6.9235 kJ/kg·K) to 10 kPa. At 10 kPa: h_f = 191.81, h_fg = 2392.1 kJ/kg, s_f = 0.6492, s_fg = 7.4996 kJ/kg·K. The isentropic efficiency is 85%. Treat the turbine as adiabatic and neglect kinetic and potential energy changes. Determine (a) the isentropic and actual specific work, (b) the actual exit quality and entropy, (c) the entropy generated per kg and the exergy destroyed per kg for T0 = 298.15 K. (d) Explain where the irreversibility comes from and why part of it is recovered in multistage turbines.
markScheme: s_gen = s2a − s1 = 0.488 kJ/kg·K (adiabatic, so all of Δs is generated)
Notes that exergy destroyed (146) is less than the work shortfall (156) because the exhaust leaves with extra exergy
Sources: friction and blade-profile losses, tip leakage, shock and wetness losses
Reheat factor: in multistage expansion, friction heating in early stages raises enthalpy available to later stages, so overall η exceeds stage η
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For isentropic expansion, s2s = s1 = 6.9235 kJ/kg·K, so x2s = (6.9235 − 0.6492)/7.4996 = 0.837. Then h2s = 191.81 + 0.837 × 2392.1 = 2193.1 kJ/kg, giving w_s = 3231.7 − 2193.1 = 1038.6 kJ/kg. The actual work is w_a = η_T w_s = 0.85 × 1038.6 = 882.8 kJ/kg.

(b) h2a = 3231.7 − 882.8 = 2348.9 kJ/kg, so x2a = (2348.9 − 191.81)/2392.1 = 0.902. Then s2a = 0.6492 + 0.902 × 7.4996 = 7.412 kJ/kg·K. The real expansion ends drier, at higher entropy, than the ideal one.

(c) The turbine is adiabatic, so s_gen = s2a − s1 = 7.412 − 6.9235 = 0.488 kJ/kg·K. By the Gouy–Stodola theorem, the exergy destroyed is T0 s_gen = 298.15 × 0.488 ≈ 146 kJ/kg. This is smaller than the work shortfall (1038.6 − 882.8 = 155.8 kJ/kg). The difference, about 10 kJ/kg, is not destroyed. It leaves with the hotter, drier exhaust as extra exergy, which a real condenser then throws away.

(d) The irreversibility comes from viscous friction in blade boundary layers and wakes, leakage over blade tips and through seals, incidence losses, and, in the wet region, droplet drag and non-equilibrium condensation. In a multistage machine, each stage's friction heats the steam, so the next stage starts at higher enthalpy and entropy, where constant-pressure lines diverge on the h–s diagram. Part of the loss is therefore recovered by later stages. This 'reheat factor' makes the overall turbine efficiency slightly higher than the individual stage efficiencies.

questions.q: A simple ideal Rankine cycle supplies 100 MW of net power. Steam leaves the boiler at 8 MPa and 500 °C (h3 = 3399.5 kJ/kg, s3 = 6.7266 kJ/kg·K), and the condenser runs at 10 kPa (h_f = 191.81 kJ/kg, v_f = 0.00101 m³/kg, h_fg = 2392.1 kJ/kg, s_f = 0.6492 kJ/kg·K, s_fg = 7.4996 kJ/kg·K). Determine (a) the pump work, (b) the turbine exit quality and work, (c) the thermal efficiency, (d) the steam mass flow rate and the rate of heat rejection. (e) Suggest two modifications to improve the cycle and explain why each works.
markScheme: Reheat: raises mean temperature of heat addition and exit quality (0.81 is low)
Regenerative feedwater heating: raises feedwater temperature, so less heat is added at low temperature
Higher boiler pressure or superheat, or lower condenser pressure, with reasoning
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Pump: w_p = v_f(p2 − p1) = 0.00101 × (8000 − 10) = 8.07 kJ/kg, so h2 = 191.81 + 8.07 = 199.9 kJ/kg.

(b) Turbine: s4 = s3, so x4 = (6.7266 − 0.6492)/7.4996 = 0.810. Then h4 = 191.81 + 0.810 × 2392.1 = 2130.3 kJ/kg and w_t = 3399.5 − 2130.3 = 1269.2 kJ/kg.

(c) Heat input: q_in = 3399.5 − 199.9 = 3199.6 kJ/kg. Net work = 1269.2 − 8.1 = 1261.1 kJ/kg, so η = 1261.1/3199.6 = 39.4%. The back work ratio is only 0.6%, which is typical of vapour cycles because pumping a liquid takes little work.

(d) ṁ = 100 000/1261.1 = 79.3 kg/s. Heat rejected per kg = h4 − h1 = 2130.3 − 191.81 = 1938.5 kJ/kg, so Q̇_out = 79.3 × 1938.5 ≈ 153.7 MW. Check: Q̇_in = 79.3 × 3199.6 = 253.7 MW, and 253.7 − 100 = 153.7 MW, so the energy balance closes.

(e) Two improvements:
- Reheat. Expand to an intermediate pressure, reheat to about 500 °C, then expand to 10 kPa. Exit quality of 0.81 would cause serious blade erosion, and reheat raises it towards 0.9. It also adds heat at a high mean temperature, which usually raises efficiency slightly.
- Regenerative feedwater heating. Steam bled from the turbine preheats the feedwater, so the boiler no longer adds heat to water at around 46 °C. This raises the mean temperature of heat addition, the main lever on Rankine efficiency. Modern plants combine several feedwater heaters with reheat and supercritical pressures.

questions.q: A gas-turbine plant runs on an air-standard Brayton cycle. Air enters the compressor at 300 K, the pressure ratio is 10, and the turbine inlet temperature is 1400 K. The compressor isentropic efficiency is 85% and the turbine's is 88%. Take c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and k = 1.4 throughout. Determine (a) the actual compressor exit and turbine exit temperatures, (b) the net specific work and the back work ratio, (c) the thermal efficiency, compared with the ideal cycle at the same pressure ratio. (d) Evaluate whether a regenerator would help this plant.
markScheme: Ideal η = 1 − 1/1.931 = 48.2%, which shows how sensitive the cycle is to component efficiencies
Regenerator: T4 (806 K) > T2 (628 K), so up to about 178 K of preheating is available, which cuts fuel input and raises η
Notes the regenerator's effectiveness, pressure drop and cost trade-offs
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The isentropic temperature ratio is 10^(0.4/1.4) = 1.931.
- Compressor: T2s = 300 × 1.931 = 579.2 K, so T2 = 300 + (579.2 − 300)/0.85 = 628.5 K.
- Turbine: T4s = 1400/1.931 = 725.1 K, so T4 = 1400 − 0.88 × (1400 − 725.1) = 806.1 K.

(b) w_c = 1.005 × (628.5 − 300) = 330.1 kJ/kg and w_t = 1.005 × (1400 − 806.1) = 596.9 kJ/kg. So w_net = 266.7 kJ/kg and the back work ratio is 330.1/596.9 = 0.553. More than half of the turbine output goes back into driving the compressor.

(c) q_in = 1.005 × (1400 − 628.5) = 775.4 kJ/kg, so η = 266.7/775.4 = 34.4%. The ideal Brayton cycle at the same pressure ratio gives 1 − 1/1.931 = 48.2%. Component losses cut efficiency by about 14 percentage points. Because the back work ratio is so high, a small loss in compressor or turbine efficiency takes a large share of the net work. Gas turbines are much more sensitive to component efficiencies than steam plants, whose back work ratio is under 1%.

(d) Regeneration uses turbine exhaust to preheat compressed air before the combustor. It is possible only if T4 > T2. Here 806 K exceeds 628.5 K, so up to about 178 K of temperature rise is available. With an ideal regenerator, q_in would fall to 1.005 × (1400 − 806.1) = 596.9 kJ/kg while w_net stayed the same, raising η to about 45%. A real regenerator (effectiveness around 0.7–0.85) gives less than this and adds pressure losses that slightly cut turbine work. At this moderate pressure ratio, regeneration is clearly worthwhile. At much higher pressure ratios T2 approaches T4, and a combined cycle would be the better use of the exhaust heat.

questions.q: A vapour-compression refrigerator using R-134a removes 10 kW from a cold store. Refrigerant leaves the evaporator as saturated vapour at −10 °C (h1 = 244.5 kJ/kg) and leaves the condenser as saturated liquid at 40 °C (h3 = 108.3 kJ/kg). An isentropic compressor would deliver it at h2s = 278.0 kJ/kg, but the real compressor has an isentropic efficiency of 80%. Determine (a) the refrigerant mass flow rate, (b) the actual compressor power and COP, (c) the condenser heat rejection rate, (d) the Carnot COP between −10 °C and 40 °C, and discuss the main sources of the gap.
markScheme: Refrigeration effect q_L = 244.5 − 108.3 = 136.2 kJ/kg; ṁ = 10/136.2 = 0.0734 kg/s
Gap: irreversible throttling instead of expansion work
Gap: desuperheating at temperatures above the condensing temperature
Gap: compressor inefficiency and finite ΔT across heat exchangers (in a full system)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The throttle is isenthalpic, so h4 = h3 = 108.3 kJ/kg. The refrigeration effect is q_L = h1 − h4 = 136.2 kJ/kg, so ṁ = 10/136.2 = 0.0734 kg/s.

(b) The actual compressor exit enthalpy is h2a = h1 + (h2s − h1)/η_C = 244.5 + 33.5/0.80 = 286.4 kJ/kg. Power = 0.0734 × (286.4 − 244.5) = 3.07 kW, giving COP_R = 10/3.07 = 3.25. With an isentropic compressor the COP would have been 136.2/33.5 = 4.07, so compressor losses alone cost about 20%.

(c) Q̇_H = ṁ(h2a − h3) = 0.0734 × 178.1 = 13.07 kW. This equals Q̇_L + Ẇ = 10 + 3.07 kW, so the first law checks.

(d) A reversible refrigerator between 263.15 K and 313.15 K has COP = 263.15/50 = 5.26. The actual cycle reaches about 62% of this. The gap comes from three places:
- Throttling is a free expansion. It destroys the work an ideal expander would recover and turns some liquid into flash vapour, which reduces the refrigeration effect.
- The compressor discharges superheated vapour. Heat is therefore rejected partly at temperatures above 40 °C, while the Carnot cycle rejects all of it at T_H.
- The compressor is irreversible.
In a real installation, the refrigerant must also run colder than the store and hotter than the ambient air to drive heat transfer, so the reservoir-based Carnot COP would be even further away. Subcooling the condensate and using economisers or multistage compression are common ways to narrow the gap.

questions.q: A rectangular sluice gate, 1.2 m wide and 2.0 m high, sits in the vertical wall of a water tank (ρ = 1000 kg/m³). It is hinged along its top edge, which is 2.0 m below the free surface, and held shut by a horizontal force P at its bottom edge. Atmosphere acts on the outer face. (a) Find the resultant hydrostatic force on the gate. (b) Find the depth of the centre of pressure. (c) Find P. (d) Explain what would happen to the centre of pressure and to P if the water level rose by a further 3 m.
markScheme: Uses gauge pressure because atmosphere acts on both sides
Higher level: F rises in proportion to h_c, and y_cp − y_c = I/(y_cA) shrinks
The centre of pressure moves towards the centroid, and P tends towards half of F (it rises, but more slowly than F)
questions.modelAnswer:
Atmospheric pressure acts on both faces, so only gauge pressure matters.

(a) The centroid depth is h_c = 2.0 + 2.0/2 = 3.0 m and the area is 2.4 m². F = ρgh_cA = 1000 × 9.81 × 3.0 × 2.4 = 70 632 N ≈ 70.6 kN, acting normal to the gate.

(b) For a rectangle, I_xc = bh³/12 = 1.2 × 2.0³/12 = 0.80 m⁴. The gate is vertical, so y = h and y_cp = h_c + I_xc/(h_cA) = 3.0 + 0.80/(3.0 × 2.4) = 3.111 m. The resultant acts 0.111 m below the centroid.

(c) Take moments about the hinge at 2.0 m depth. The water force acts 1.111 m below the hinge and P acts 2.0 m below it. P × 2.0 = 70.63 × 1.111, so P = 39.2 kN.

(d) If the surface rises 3 m, h_c = 6.0 m, so F doubles to 141.3 kN. The offset I_xc/(h_cA) = 0.80/14.4 = 0.056 m halves. The centre of pressure is now 0.056 m below the centroid, which is 1.056 m below the hinge, and P = 141.3 × 1.056/2.0 = 74.6 kN. P roughly doubles, but its share of F falls from 0.556 towards 0.5. This happens because the pressure distribution becomes more uniform relative to its mean as depth increases. A useful general point for design: the deeper a gate, the closer its load acts to the centroid.

questions.q: A horizontal venturi meter in a water main (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) has an inlet diameter of 150 mm and a throat diameter of 75 mm. A mercury (ρ = 13 600 kg/m³) U-tube connected between inlet and throat shows a 180 mm difference in levels. The discharge coefficient is 0.98. (a) Find the pressure difference. (b) Derive the flow equation from Bernoulli and continuity and find the actual flow rate. (c) Explain why the discharge coefficient is less than 1 and why venturis are preferred to orifice plates despite their cost.
markScheme: Bernoulli (z1 = z2): p1 − p2 = ρ(V2² − V1²)/2
C_d < 1 because of viscous losses and non-uniform velocity profiles; venturi has a gradual diffuser, so permanent pressure loss is small (about 10–20% of Δp) versus about 60% or more for an orifice
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The manometer gives Δp = (ρ_m − ρ_w)gΔh = 12 600 × 9.81 × 0.18 = 22 249 Pa ≈ 22.2 kPa.

(b) Apply Bernoulli between the inlet (1) and the throat (2), at the same height: p1 − p2 = ρ(V2² − V1²)/2. Continuity gives V1 = V2(A2/A1) = V2β², with β = d2/d1 = 0.5. Substituting:

Δp = ρV2²(1 − β⁴)/2, so V2 = √[2Δp/(ρ(1 − β⁴))].

With 1 − β⁴ = 0.9375, V2 = √(2 × 22 249/937.5) = 6.89 m/s. The throat area is π × 0.075²/4 = 4.418 × 10⁻³ m², so Q_ideal = 0.0304 m³/s and Q_actual = C_d Q_ideal = 0.98 × 0.0304 = 0.0298 m³/s, about 29.8 L/s. As a check, the inlet velocity is 1.69 m/s, which is reasonable for a water main.

(c) Bernoulli ignores viscosity. In reality friction in the converging section reduces the throat velocity slightly, and the velocity profiles are not uniform. The measured flow is therefore a little below ideal, which C_d captures through calibration. A venturi's smooth contraction keeps C_d close to 1, and its gentle diffuser recovers most of the pressure, so the permanent head loss is only a small fraction of the measured Δp. A sharp-edged orifice is cheap and compact, but its flow separates and forms a vena contracta, so C_d is about 0.6. Most of its differential pressure is lost as turbulence, which costs pumping energy continuously. In large water or process mains, a venturi's energy savings over the years usually outweigh its higher purchase cost.

questions.q: A horizontal nozzle is bolted to the end of a fire hose. It reduces the bore from 80 mm to 25 mm and discharges water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) at 0.015 m³/s as a free jet to atmosphere. Neglect losses and the weight of water. (a) Find the inlet and jet velocities. (b) Find the gauge pressure at the nozzle inlet. (c) Use the momentum equation to find the magnitude and direction of the force the water exerts on the nozzle, and hence the load on the bolts. (d) Explain why firefighters feel a backward reaction, and reconcile this with your answer to (c).
markScheme: Bernoulli with p2 = 0 gauge: p1 = ρ(V2² − V1²)/2 ≈ 462 kPa gauge
Control volume around the water in the nozzle, x in the flow direction
R_x = −1911 N (the nozzle pushes the water upstream)
The water pushes the nozzle downstream with 1.91 kN, which the bolts must resist in tension
The momentum flux increase is much smaller than the inlet pressure force
Reaction on the firefighter: consider a control volume including the hose upstream, with the jet momentum ρQV2 = 458 N giving a net backward thrust
Distinguishes the nozzle-joint force from the reaction on the whole hose and nozzle system
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A1 = π × 0.08²/4 = 5.027 × 10⁻³ m² and A2 = π × 0.025²/4 = 4.909 × 10⁻⁴ m². So V1 = 0.015/A1 = 2.98 m/s and V2 = 0.015/A2 = 30.56 m/s.

(b) The jet is at atmospheric pressure (p2 = 0 gauge) and losses are neglected, so p1 = ρ(V2² − V1²)/2 = 500 × (933.8 − 8.9) = 462 kPa gauge.

(c) Take the water inside the nozzle as the control volume, with x positive downstream. The forces on it are p1A1 at the inlet (gauge), zero at the outlet, and R_x from the nozzle wall. The momentum equation gives:

p1A1 + R_x = ρQ(V2 − V1)
2324 + R_x = 1000 × 0.015 × 27.57 = 413.6 N
R_x = −1911 N

The nozzle pushes the water upstream with 1.91 kN. By Newton's third law, the water pushes the nozzle downstream with 1.91 kN. The bolts at the hose coupling must hold the nozzle on, in tension, against about 1.9 kN. Most of this comes from the high inlet pressure acting on the contracting walls, which the relatively small rise in momentum does not balance.

(d) A firefighter holds the hose as well as the nozzle. For a control volume that includes the hose upstream, cut where the water flows slowly and the pressure is balanced by the hose wall tension, the net external force needed is set mainly by the momentum leaving in the jet, ρQV2 = 1000 × 0.015 × 30.56 = 458 N. That force points backward, like the thrust of a rocket. The coupling bolts carry a forward internal force, but the person feels the net backward reaction of the whole hose and nozzle system. The two answers are consistent because they come from different control volumes.

questions.q: Moortown Water pumps 0.02 m³/s of water (ρ = 998 kg/m³, μ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s) from a low reservoir to a high reservoir whose free surface is 20 m higher. The pipeline is 500 m of 100 mm commercial steel (ε = 0.045 mm). The sum of minor loss coefficients, including entrance, bends, valves and exit, is 5.0. Both reservoirs are open to atmosphere. (a) Find the mean velocity and Reynolds number. (b) Find the friction factor, stating your method. (c) Find the friction and minor head losses. (d) Find the pump head required and the electrical power for an overall pump efficiency of 75%. (e) The utility considers using a 125 mm pipe instead. Discuss qualitatively the effect on head loss and the economic trade-off.
markScheme: Colebrook iteration (or Haaland / Moody chart) gives f ≈ 0.018
Energy equation between free surfaces: H_p = Δz + h_f + h_m = 51.7 m
Friction dominates: about 58% of the pump head
At fixed Q, h_f ∝ roughly 1/D⁵, so 125 mm cuts friction loss to roughly a third
Trade-off: higher capital cost of a larger pipe vs lower lifetime pumping energy; optimum economic diameter
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A = π × 0.1²/4 = 7.854 × 10⁻³ m², so V = 0.02/A = 2.55 m/s. Re = ρVD/μ = 998 × 2.546 × 0.1/0.001 = 2.54 × 10⁵. The flow is fully turbulent.

(b) ε/D = 0.045/100 = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴. Solving Colebrook, 1/√f = −2 log10[(ε/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re√f)], by iteration from f = 0.02 converges to f = 0.0182. Haaland gives 0.0180 and the Moody chart about 0.018.

(c) The velocity head is V²/2g = 2.546²/19.62 = 0.330 m. Friction loss: h_f = f(L/D)(V²/2g) = 0.0182 × 5000 × 0.330 = 30.0 m. Minor losses: h_m = 5.0 × 0.330 = 1.65 m.

(d) Apply the energy equation between the two free surfaces. Both are at atmospheric pressure with negligible velocity, so H_p = Δz + h_f + h_m = 20 + 30.0 + 1.65 = 51.7 m. The electrical power is P = ρgQH/η = 998 × 9.81 × 0.02 × 51.7/0.75 = 13.5 kW. The pump is mostly fighting friction, not lifting water.

(e) At fixed Q, V ∝ 1/D² and h_f ∝ fV²/D, so h_f varies roughly as 1/D⁵ (a little less, because f changes slightly). Moving to 125 mm would cut V to about 1.63 m/s and friction loss to roughly 10 m. Pump head would fall to about 31 m, and power to about 8 kW. The larger pipe costs more to buy and lay, but saves around 5 kW of continuous pumping, which adds up over a 30–50 year life. The economic diameter minimises total annualised cost (capital plus energy). Rising energy prices and carbon costs push that optimum towards larger diameters. Lower velocities also reduce erosion and the pressure surges from water hammer.

questions.q: Oil (ρ = 900 kg/m³, μ = 0.10 Pa·s) flows through a 10 m long horizontal tube of 20 mm bore at 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s. (a) Find the mean velocity and Reynolds number and identify the regime. (b) Find the pressure drop in two ways: from Hagen–Poiseuille and from Darcy–Weisbach with the appropriate friction factor. (c) Find the pumping power. (d) State the maximum velocity and explain how the pressure drop would change if the oil were heated so that its viscosity halved.
markScheme: Δp ∝ μ in laminar flow: halving μ halves Δp (still laminar, Re ≈ 115)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A = π × 0.02²/4 = 3.142 × 10⁻⁴ m², so V = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴/3.142 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.318 m/s. Re = ρVD/μ = 900 × 0.318 × 0.02/0.10 = 57.3. This is well below 2300, so the flow is laminar.

(b) Hagen–Poiseuille: Δp = 128μLQ/(πD⁴) = 128 × 0.10 × 10 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁴/(π × 1.6 × 10⁻⁷) = 25.5 kPa. Darcy–Weisbach: f = 64/Re = 64/57.3 = 1.117, so Δp = f(L/D)(ρV²/2) = 1.117 × 500 × (900 × 0.1013/2) = 25.5 kPa. The two methods agree, as they should, because f = 64/Re is derived from the Hagen–Poiseuille solution.

(c) Pumping power = QΔp = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 25 465 = 2.55 W, which is tiny. Viscous oil lines are often designed around starting pressure rather than running power.

(d) The laminar profile is parabolic, so the centreline velocity is u_max = 2V = 0.64 m/s. At fixed Q, Hagen–Poiseuille shows Δp ∝ μ. Halving the viscosity halves the pressure drop to about 12.7 kPa. Re doubles to about 115, so the flow stays laminar. This direct proportionality is why heavy fuel oil and crude lines are often heated or trace-heated: oil viscosity falls steeply with temperature, so modest heating greatly reduces pumping requirements. In turbulent flow, by contrast, Δp depends only weakly on μ.

questions.q: A counterflow heat exchanger cools 2.0 kg/s of oil (c_p = 2.1 kJ/kg·K) entering at 150 °C, using 1.5 kg/s of water (c_p = 4.18 kJ/kg·K) entering at 20 °C. The overall heat transfer coefficient is 300 W/m²·K and the area is 40 m². (a) Use the ε-NTU method to find the heat duty and both outlet temperatures. (b) Check your result with the LMTD method. (c) Explain why ε-NTU is the natural method here. (d) After a year in service, fouling adds a resistance of 0.0005 m²·K/W. Discuss qualitatively how the duty changes, and critically evaluate the strategies an engineer might use to manage fouling.
markScheme: C_h = 4.2 kW/K, C_c = 6.27 kW/K; C_min = C_h (oil), C_r = 0.670
Counterflow ε = [1 − exp(−NTU(1 − C_r))]/[1 − C_r exp(−NTU(1 − C_r))] = 0.826
ε-NTU suits rating problems where outlet temperatures are unknown; LMTD would need iteration
Fouling: 1/U' = 1/300 + 0.0005, so U' = 261 W/m²·K, NTU falls to 2.49, ε falls (about 0.79), duty drops by about 4%
Strategies: design margin or excess area, higher velocities, chemical treatment and filtration, cleaning schedules; evaluates costs and side effects
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Heat capacity rates: C_h = 2.0 × 2.1 = 4.2 kW/K and C_c = 1.5 × 4.18 = 6.27 kW/K. So C_min = 4.2 kW/K (the oil) and C_r = 0.670. NTU = UA/C_min = 0.3 × 40/4.2 = 2.857. For counterflow:

ε = [1 − exp(−NTU(1 − C_r))]/[1 − C_r exp(−NTU(1 − C_r))] = (1 − e^(−0.943))/(1 − 0.670e^(−0.943)) = 0.826.

Q̇_max = 4.2 × (150 − 20) = 546 kW, so Q̇ = 451 kW. Oil outlet: 150 − 451/4.2 = 42.6 °C. Water outlet: 20 + 451/6.27 = 91.9 °C.

(b) The terminal differences are 150 − 91.9 = 58.1 K and 42.6 − 20 = 22.6 K. ΔT_lm = (58.1 − 22.6)/ln(58.1/22.6) = 37.6 K, so UAΔT_lm = 12 × 37.6 = 451 kW, which agrees exactly. The water leaves hotter than the oil outlet, which is possible only in counterflow (a temperature cross).

(c) This is a rating problem: the exchanger is given and the outlets are unknown. LMTD would need guessed outlet temperatures and iteration, whereas ε-NTU gives the duty directly.

(d) With fouling, 1/U' = 1/300 + 0.0005 = 0.003833, so U' = 261 W/m²·K. NTU falls to 2.49 and ε to about 0.79, cutting the duty by around 4%, to about 433 kW. The oil leaves at about 47 °C. The effect is modest here because the clean U is already low. In a water–water exchanger with U around 2000 W/m²·K, the same fouling resistance would halve U.

There are four main ways to manage fouling:
- Oversizing the area: simple, but it lowers clean-condition velocities, which can speed up fouling.
- Keeping tube-side velocities high (around 1–2 m/s): reduces deposition, at a pumping cost.
- Water treatment and filtration: tackles scaling and biofouling at source, but brings chemical and environmental costs.
- Planned cleaning: mechanical or chemical, possibly with on-line ball systems. This means downtime or duplicate units.
A good engineer weighs the lost duty and energy against these costs, often using monitoring of U over time to optimise the cleaning interval rather than relying on generic fouling factors.

questions.q: 'Energy is conserved in every process, so engineers should talk about the degradation of energy, not its loss.' Critically discuss this statement with reference to entropy generation, exergy and second-law efficiency. Illustrate your answer with at least two engineering examples.
markScheme: First law: energy is conserved, so 'energy loss' in everyday language really means conversion to less useful forms
Second law: entropy generation measures irreversibility (S_gen ≥ 0)
Exergy defined relative to a dead state (T0, p0); exergy is not conserved
Gouy–Stodola: exergy destroyed = T0 S_gen, linking degradation to lost work
Second-law efficiency compares actual performance with the reversible limit; it can reveal waste hidden by high first-law efficiencies
Example: a gas boiler ~90% first-law efficient but low exergetic efficiency, because high-temperature combustion is used to make low-temperature heat; a heat pump does better
Example: a throttle valve conserves enthalpy but destroys exergy; or heat transfer across a large ΔT in a heat exchanger
Example: a power-plant condenser rejects a lot of energy but little exergy, so the boiler, not the condenser, is the main exergy sink
Qualifies the claim: some energy is genuinely lost to a system boundary (e.g. heat leaks), and it is still useful to call that a loss
Reasoned conclusion on terminology and on engineering decision-making
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement is right that 'energy loss' is loose language. The first law guarantees that energy is conserved in any process, so what engineers call a loss is energy leaving the system of interest or changing into a less useful form. The second law gives that intuition a precise measure.

Every real process generates entropy (S_gen > 0) through friction, mixing, unrestrained expansion or heat transfer across a finite temperature difference. Exergy is the maximum work obtainable as a system comes to equilibrium with its environment at T0, p0. Unlike energy, exergy is destroyed by irreversibility, and the Gouy–Stodola theorem quantifies this: X_dest = T0 S_gen. 'Degradation' therefore has an exact meaning. It is the destruction of exergy, the loss of the capacity to do work.

This matters for design.
- A domestic gas boiler may reach 90% first-law efficiency, yet it uses flame temperatures near 2000 K to make water at about 330 K. Its exergetic efficiency is only around 10–15%. A heat pump delivering the same heat from electricity does far better in second-law terms, which is why heat pumps feature in decarbonisation policy.
- In a steam plant, the condenser rejects about 60% of the energy input but very little exergy, because that heat is near ambient temperature. The largest exergy destruction is in the boiler, where heat moves across hundreds of kelvin from combustion gases to steam. A first-law analysis points at the wrong component; a second-law analysis points at the right one.
- A throttling valve conserves enthalpy exactly but destroys exergy, which is why high-pressure letdown in gas networks is a target for expansion turbines.

The statement does need qualifying. From the viewpoint of a specific system, energy really does cross the boundary as heat leaks or exhaust, and calling that a loss is legitimate and useful for energy accounting. Exergy also depends on the chosen dead state, which brings in some ambiguity.

On balance, 'degradation' is the more accurate concept, and second-law efficiency is the better guide for engineering decisions. First-law efficiencies still have their place in bookkeeping.
